{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.01256v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "DEFA: DEPENDENCY-GUIDEDFAILUREATTRIBUTION
FORLLM AGENTS
Bo Deng1,2 Xinlei Zheng2 Yi Wei2
Kang Zhou1 Chongyang Tao2 Renzhao Liang2
Xuanren Chen2 Lifan Guo1 Chi Zhang1
1Qwen DianJin Team, Alibaba Cloud Computing
2Beihang University
ABSTRACT
Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated
by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both
step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided
framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations
and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajec-
tory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their
sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally,
DeFA uses step evidence and the steps’ roles in failure propagation to identify the
decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories,
DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment’s
detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis ac-
cess to global execution context. Across Who&When and the Who&When Pro
text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accu-
racy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among
taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video tra-
jectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations
support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the
failure propagation graph. Using DeFA’s diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in
Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6–15 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improve-
ment on subsequent tasks.
1 INTRODUCTION
When an LLM agent fails a task, the final outcome rarely reveals which earlier decision was respon-

{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18126v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM
Decisions Already Made
Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
Abstract
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-
ment it is made; the action it commits to is la-
tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We
therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci-
sion validity and a decision ledger that realises
it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh-
ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence
guarantees at action time, placing the remain-
ing risk in information published afterwards.
Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities:
routing, which delivers that information to af-
fected decisions before their revision deadlines,
and temporal judgment, which reads it for the
time of action. The ledger is persistent state
holding each decision’s times, evidence and
background knowledge, indexed by watch con-
ditions written at decision time. Controlled
decision streams with exact labels confirm four
predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron-
tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the
accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de-
cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows
routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing
reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect
dependencies at low exposure; and the remain-
ing errors concern when a change takes effect.
Freshness makes a decision right when it is
made; routing and temporal judgment keep it
right when it is carried out.
1 Introduction
At 13:05, a user asks an assistant for a walk-in din-
ner at 20:30. The assistant chooses Lovage Corner,
the best-rated restaurant within walking distance,
in the Bellhaven district. At 18:40, the grid op-
erator announces emergency works at the Gorran
substation from 19:50, leaving every area it sup-
plies without power; the Gorran substation supplies
the Bellhaven district (Figure 1). The choice was
right at 13:05 and is wrong at 20:30. The informa-
tion that settles it appeared after the decision and
refers to the restaurant only through the substation
revision window

works at the
Gorran substation

{"url": "https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1515/", "scope": "extracted web-page text; may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Where Confabulation Lives: Latent Feature Discovery in LLMs - ACL Anthology
Where Confabulation Lives: Latent Feature Discovery in
LLM
s
Thibaud Ardoin
,
Yi Cai
,
Gerhard Wunder
Abstract
Hallucination remains a critical failure mode of large language models (LLMs), undermining their trustworthiness in real-world applications. In this work, we focus on confabulation, a foundational aspect of hallucination where the model fabricates facts about unknown entities. We introduce a targeted dataset designed to isolate and analyze this behavior across diverse prompt types. Using this dataset, and building on recent progress in interpreting LLM internals, we extract latent directions associated with confabulation using sparse projections. A simple vector-based steering method demonstrates that these directions can modulate model behavior with minimal disruption, shedding light on the inner representations that drive factual and non-factual output. Our findings contribute to a deeper mechanistic understanding of LLMs and pave the way toward more trustworthy and controllable generation. We release the code and dataset at
https://github.com/Thibaud-Ardoin/where-confabulation-lives
.
